summary_html: A **child is removed without exigency or warrant**, violating constitutional rights. Federal courts treat such removals as seizures under the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments, actionable via §1983.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — limits removals to lawful emergencies and requires judicial review  
- **U.S. Constitution (4th & 14th Amendments)** — protects family integrity; requires due process

primary_citations.citation_text: Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2223 — Reporting of certain abuse or neglect of children; persons required to report (Revised Kansas Code for Care of Children, ch. 38, art. 22)
Chapter 38 — Minors; Article 22, Revised Kansas Code for Care of Children (child welfare primary)

regulations_applicable.title: Agency 30 - KANSAS DEPARTMENT FOR CHILDREN AND FAMILIES

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Roska ex rel. Roska v. Peterson
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that caseworkers who entered a family's home and removed a child without a warrant, court order, or exigent circumstances violated the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments, rejecting the argument that the 'special needs' doctrine excuses the warrant requirement for child welfare removals.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading Tenth Circuit authority for a § 1983 wrongful-removal claim arising from a warrantless, non-exigent removal, which controls in Kansas.
key_cases.quote: We find no special need that renders the warrant requirement impracticable when social workers enter a home to remove a child, absent exigent circumstances

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: In a case beginning with an anonymous hotline call, the court affirmed the denial of qualified immunity to the child welfare specialist and the officer who directed a six-year-old's seizure and transport from school for questioning, while reversing as to the officer who merely transported the child and as to the Fourteenth Amendment familial association claim.
key_cases.relevance: This is a recent Tenth Circuit decision allowing a § 1983 unlawful seizure claim against a child welfare worker to proceed past qualified immunity.
key_cases.quote: The district court correctly determined that two of the three defendants were not entitled to qualified immunity on the Fourth Amendment unlawful seizure claim

key_cases.case_name: Lowther v. Children, Youth & Families Department
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed qualified immunity for an investigator and county defendants on a warrantless-entry claim, holding that under circuit precedent a reasonable official could believe reasonable suspicion of past abuse justified warrantless entry, so the law was not clearly established to the contrary.
key_cases.relevance: Read together with Roska, this decision shows how narrow the clearly-established path is for a Kansas plaintiff's warrantless-entry claim today.
key_cases.quote: a reasonable investigator or officer could reasonably believe warrantless entry was justified by reasonable suspicion of past abuse

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed dismissal on qualified immunity of Fourth Amendment claims brought over a caseworker's warrantless visual body search of a four-year-old at school without parental consent, holding that the law was not clearly established that the special needs doctrine could not justify such a search, and affirmed dismissal of the parents' Fourteenth Amendment claims.
key_cases.relevance: The circuit's unresolved treatment of the special needs doctrine means many investigative-search claims in Kansas will fail on qualified immunity rather than on the merits.
key_cases.quote: the Does have not shown that Ms. Woodard's search violated clearly established Fourth Amendment law

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that an unwed father was entitled as a matter of due process to a hearing on his fitness before his children could be taken from him, and that Illinois' presumption of unfitness applied only to unwed fathers denied him equal protection.
key_cases.relevance: This is the foundational federal holding that removal without an individualized hearing violates due process, on which wrongful-removal claims ultimately rest.
key_cases.quote: as a matter of due process of law, Stanley was entitled to a hearing on his fitness as a parent before his children were taken from him
